idiom_name: extension function/property backed by a WeakHashMap (or identity-keyed) side table
implementation_notes: Kotlin's native answer for the interface half is the extension function and the extension property: declared outside the class, resolved statically, callable as if they were members, and invisible to clients that do not import them. The state half has no language support - the documentation states that 'since extensions don't actually add members to classes, there's no efficient way for an extension property to have a backing field, [so] initializers are not allowed' - and the canonical replacement is exactly the pattern's registry in miniature: the official example backs an extension property with mutableMapOf<House, Int>() and computes the attribute from the map. In production use WeakHashMap (map lives beside the subject) or an IdentityHashMap wrapper when the subject overrides equals; keep the map private to the file that owns the capability and expose the capability check through a nullable or sealed result instead of a raw map read.
pitfalls: Extension properties cannot have backing fields or initializers, so two extensions declared in different files that both lazily create state will silently maintain two independent copies unless they share one map.

WeakHashMap is not thread-safe, its entries vanish when the key is collected (caching a strong reference to the value defeats it), and it uses equals/hashCode - a subject with value-based equality collapses distinct instances into one entry; wrap the key or use an identity map.

Members always win over extensions with the same signature, so adding a member to the class later silently changes which code runs at existing call sites; and a top-level extension is visible to every file in the module, which is why capability extensions belong in the package that owns the capability.
